old: Originating from the physical sensors of electronic keyboards and pianos, MIDI velocity is a machine-centric measurement of physical intensity. To say it operates as a "note-level" parameter means that every music note from a discrete key strike is assigned an independent, static integer representing its initial strike force. This strict per-note measurement dictates that velocity functions as a discrete loudness control parameter. It is highly granular and absolute within its own scale, yet the resulting loudness highly depends on the acoustic environment and the specific instrument being played. Because MIDI velocity is necessary for MIDI-to-audio playback in DAWs and synthesisers, a common default is set to 64 when it is missing.
new: Here, MIDI velocity refers to the velocity value in a Note On message. It is a machine-readable control parameter. In sensor-equipped piano data, the recorded value acts as a discretised proxy for key or hammer motion. Each note carries an integer value that can be edited independently, although its acoustic effect depends on the instrument and renderer. When expressive values are missing, a MIDI sequence may instead use a constant such as 64.

old: Two limitations of waveform-level supervision are relevant here. First, a Diff-Synth only approximates the real instrument; its waveform statistics differ from real recordings in timbre, articulation, microphone response, and room acoustics. A waveform or spectral loss therefore spends much of its gradient budget on residual mismatch rather than on velocity-dependent behaviour. Second, an instrument-specific Diff-Synth requires a dedicated design: piano-oriented synthesisers expect piano-specific controls such as pedal state, while guitar-oriented synthesisers expect string-wise trajectories. Reusing one Diff-Synth across instruments is therefore impractical.
new: Two limitations of waveform-level supervision are relevant here. First, a Diff-Synth only approximates the real instrument; its waveform statistics differ from real recordings in timbre, articulation, microphone response, and room acoustics. A waveform or spectral loss can be influenced by residual mismatch as well as velocity-dependent behaviour. Second, an instrument-specific Diff-Synth requires a dedicated design: piano-oriented synthesisers expect piano-specific controls such as pedal state, while guitar-oriented synthesisers expect string-wise trajectories. Reusing one Diff-Synth across instruments is therefore impractical.

old: Third, the asymmetry between the two adaptation interfaces widens with crop length. On FL dataset, Diff-Synth's $r_{\mathrm{BSSL}}$ falls by $0.083$ when moving from $2$\,s to $5$\,s, while Diff-SFProxy's $r_{\mathrm{BSSL}}$ varies within $0.01$. Longer crops give waveform-level objectives more of the underlying timbral mismatch to fit, while parameter-level supervision sees only per-note targets and is therefore much less sensitive to crop length. This mirrors a long-standing observation in inverse-problem design: a supervision signal that only depends on the latent variable of interest is more stable than a high-dimensional signal that mixes that variable with many nuisance factors.

old: Velocity is not the only MIDI control that shapes rendered dynamics: continuous controllers can also encode within-note loudness variation~\cite{ryu2024midfild}. Pedal settings and room response also affect the synthesised piano waveform and are explicitly modelled by DDSP-Piano~\cite{renault2023ddsp_piano}. Consequently, when adaptation updates only velocity, the velocity gradient can become entangled with residuals caused by fixed or unobserved controls. Diff-SFProxy avoids this contamination by treating velocity as the only loudness-shaping degree of freedom, but the choice carries its own cost. The recovered velocity absorbs effects that, in the real performance, came from other parallel controls.
new: Velocity is not the only MIDI control that shapes rendered dynamics: continuous controllers can also encode within-note loudness variation~\cite{ryu2024midfild}. Pedal settings and room response also affect the synthesised piano waveform and are explicitly modelled by DDSP-Piano~\cite{renault2023ddsp_piano}. Consequently, when adaptation updates only velocity, the velocity gradient can become entangled with residuals caused by fixed or unobserved controls. Diff-SFProxy restricts the adapted control to velocity, but this does not remove effects of unobserved controls from the target audio. The recovered velocity may therefore absorb effects that, in the real performance, came from other parallel controls.
